asset_title: How Much Recruiters Actually Make Per Hire: Commission Rates by Recruiter Type in 2026
distinct_angle: Breaks down what 'per hire' pay really means across agency/contingency, retained, RPO, and in-house recruiters, with real commission percentages and dollar ranges by role and seniority from public salary and industry-fee data, answering the recruiter's-own-earnings question the keyword actually asks instead of restating employer cost-per-hire.

verdicts.item: how much does an it recruiter make
verdicts.reason: Only a single commission-rate range for tech/IT roles is given, with no base salary, dollar example, or seniority breakdown specific to IT recruiters — too thin for a full section.
verdicts.evidence: By role type (Quora/hrands): tech and IT roles pay 15–33% commission based on volume or billings; executive search roles pay 30–35% as a percentage of the agency's charged fee[13].

verdicts.item: recruiter salary
verdicts.reason: Dossier has a dedicated Base Salary Benchmarks section with multiple sourced figures, ranges, and city breakdowns, clearly separated from commission/fee discussion.
verdicts.evidence: Glassdoor puts the average US base recruiter salary at $52,657 per year, with offers commonly ranging from $35,000 up to $170,000 for Director of Talent and other senior roles[11].

verdicts.item: how do recruiters get paid
verdicts.reason: Dossier explains both the agency-fee mechanisms (six commission structures: contingency, retained, flat, hourly/daily, temp markup, temp-to-perm) and how individual recruiters are paid internally (base-plus-commission splits, draw-against-commission, escalating tiers), giving ample concrete material for a full section.
verdicts.evidence: The most common recruiting compensation model pairs a base salary with commission, with a standard 60:40 ratio — 60% base salary, 40% commission[13].

verdicts.item: how do job placement agencies make money
verdicts.reason: Dossier extensively details the fee structures agencies use to generate revenue, including contingency, retained, flat-fee, markup, and conversion models with real percentages and dollar amounts.
verdicts.evidence: Recruitment and staffing agencies convert placements into revenue through roughly six distinct fee structures, including contingency search, retained search, contract/temp markups, flat fees, hourly/daily rates, and temp-to-perm conversion fees, which together accounted for virtually all of the $189 billion the U.S. staffing and recruiting industry generated in 2024[1].

verdicts.item: recruitment consultant earnings
verdicts.reason: The dossier gives detailed agency/consultant commission structures, ratios, and worked payout examples across seniority, region, and role type.
verdicts.evidence: External/agency recruiters are typically paid a percentage of the placed candidate's first-year salary, most often cited as 20–30%[11], though other benchmarks narrow this to 15–25% (with 20% as the standard benchmark for contingency search) and 25–35% for retained executive search[1].

verdicts.item: RPO recruiter fees
verdicts.reason: Dossier gives concrete RPO fee models and dollar/percentage ranges (hourly billing, placement fee combo, and the three RPO variants with pricing), enough to write a specific section.
verdicts.evidence: RPO (Recruitment Process Outsourcing) fees are typically billed hourly at $100-$200 per hour[3], sometimes combined with a smaller placement fee of $2,500-$5,000 once a role is filled to align incentives between quick and delayed placements[3]; RPO variants price differently by scope — Project RPO uses cost-per-hire for a defined burst of roles, Selective RPO uses a monthly retainer plus cost-per-hire for an ongoing segment, and Full RPO uses a monthly management fee with volume-based pricing tiers[1].

verdicts.item: contingency recruiter fee percentage
verdicts.reason: Dossier gives detailed contingency fee percentages, benchmarks, and worked dollar examples across multiple sections.
verdicts.evidence: Contingency search is a "pay-for-performance" arrangement in which an agency is compensated only if it fills the role, typically for 15% to 30% of the hire's first-year salary, with 20% often cited as the industry benchmark; it requires no upfront payment but is non-exclusive, so recruiters may compete with rival firms and abandon difficult searches for easier ones[2][1][5].
